⚠️ SPOILER ALERT: This review contains detailed plot analysis and may reveal key story elements.
🚨 WOKE TRAP WARNING

This film draws you in for a significant portion of its runtime with traditional or neutral content before springing its woke agenda. Know before you go!

Conservative fans of the original Arnold Schwarzenegger film will walk in expecting a spiritual successor and instead find a movie that has more in common with How to Train Your Dragon than the 1987 classic. The bait is real. Proceed with caution.

Overall Perspective

Dan Trachtenberg clearly loves the Predator franchise. That much is obvious. With Badlands, his third Predator project in three years, he swings for the fences by making the Predator himself the protagonist for the first time in franchise history. It is a bold creative decision. It is also a decision that opens the door to every Disney instinct that conservative audiences have learned to dread.

The setup is genuinely promising. Dek is a Yautja runt, the undersized son of clan leader Njohrr, who wants to prove himself. When Njohrr orders Dek killed for being too weak, Dek's older brother Kwei sacrifices himself to get Dek off-world. That is a strong opening. The fraternal sacrifice, the tyrannical father, the exile with something to prove.

Then Dek crash-lands on the planet Genna and immediately loses all his weapons. Because the movie needs him stripped of his Predator gear so he can be dependent on Thia, a damaged Weyland-Yutani android played by Elle Fanning. And this is where things go sideways.

Thia is not just Dek's guide. She is his moral teacher, his emotional therapist, and his philosophical compass. She teaches him that strength means something different than what his violent, patriarchal clan taught him. She is the female character who exists to civilize the toxic masculine protagonist. If you have watched any Disney property in the last decade, you know this character.

The pattern extends beyond Thia. Every helpful character in Dek's new life is female. Thia guides him. Bud, a cute alien creature, is female. Bud's parent, the Kalisk, is a single mother. Meanwhile, Dek's entire biological family, all male, ranges from murderous to dead. The message is not subtle. Your male family is toxic. Your real family is the women you meet along the way.

Bud deserves special attention because Bud is the clearest symptom of the Disneyfication of the Predator franchise. This is a creature designed to sell toys. In a franchise built on the terror of an alien hunter stalking human soldiers through a jungle, the introduction of a cuddly sidekick represents a fundamental genre shift.

The PG-13 rating confirms the shift. Every previous standalone Predator film carried an R rating. Badlands is the first to go PG-13. The horror element that defined the franchise is completely absent. What replaces it is a coming-of-age buddy comedy between a sulky alien teenager and a wisecracking robot.

To Trachtenberg's credit, the film looks fantastic. The visual effects are genuinely impressive. Genna feels like a real alien ecosystem. The fight choreography has real weight and creativity. Elle Fanning commits fully to a dual performance bringing more depth than the script deserves.

But the ideological architecture is impossible to ignore. Dek's entire arc is about rejecting masculine authority and embracing a feminine-coded found family. Strength, hierarchy, competition, the warrior ethos are treated as symptoms of toxic masculinity rather than values worth preserving.

There are traditional elements worth acknowledging. The brother's sacrifice is genuinely moving and operates on entirely traditional terms. Dek's determination to prove himself echoes classic underdog narratives. The final confrontation with his father has real dramatic weight.

Conservative viewers should understand exactly what this film is. It is the Disneyfication of one of the last major R-rated action franchises. The PG-13 rating, the cute sidekick, the feminist messaging, the defanged male lead, and the found-family-over-blood-family thesis are all Disney's house style applied to a property that was built on the opposite values. The craft is real. The agenda is equally real. And the franchise you grew up with is not coming back.

Woke Trap Warning

Trap Present: Yes — Degree: significant. This film disguises its ideological payload inside a franchise that conservative audiences associate with hyper-masculine action. The trailers sell a Predator origin story with alien world-building and brutal combat. What arrives is a Disney-sanitized adventure with heavy feminist messaging, a PG-13 rating (a franchise first), cute sidekick merchandising bait, and a systematic pattern of male villainy versus female virtue.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Dan Trachtenberg

MODERATE PROGRESSIVE

Talented genre filmmaker who has progressively absorbed Disney's house style. The trajectory from the neutral 10 Cloverfield Lane to the moderately progressive Prey to the overtly progressive Badlands tracks with his deepening relationship with Disney/20th Century Studios.

Writer: Patrick Aison

Wrote the screenplay for both Prey and Badlands. Television credits include Treadstone and Kingdom. The feminist messaging in Badlands suggests either Aison's own progressive inclinations or significant creative direction from Trachtenberg and Disney.

Producers

  • John Davis (Davis Entertainment) — One of Hollywood's most prolific producers. Credits include the original Predator (1987). Commercial producer who follows the market.
  • Dan Trachtenberg — See director profile. As producer on his own film, his creative vision is undiluted.
  • Ben Rosenblatt — Long-time Trachtenberg collaborator. Production work is Trachtenberg-adjacent.
  • Lawrence Gordon — Executive Producer. Legendary producer of the original Predator and Die Hard. Now in his 90s, likely a legacy/rights position.

Fidelity Casting Analysis N/A

Original sci-fi setting with no historical or source-material casting benchmarks.

Predator: Badlands is set on alien worlds with a cast consisting primarily of CGI aliens and synthetic androids. No historical or literary source material creates casting fidelity benchmarks. Physical casting was driven by practical needs: Dimitrius Schuster-Koloamatangi (Samoan descent) for creature suit performance, Reuben de Jong (7'1" Dutch former kickboxer) for physical size.

Adult Viewer Insight

Conservative adult viewers should approach Predator: Badlands with clear eyes about what it is and what it is not. It is not a Predator film in the tradition of the 1987 original. It is a Disney family adventure film wearing the Predator franchise's skin. The feminist messaging is persistent but not as suffocating as the worst examples of modern Disney output. The brother's sacrifice in the opening act is powerful enough to carry you through the film's softer stretches. The real concern is not this individual film but the trajectory it represents. The Predator franchise has been systematically transformed from R-rated masculine action horror into PG-13 family entertainment with progressive gender messaging. If you value the franchise as it was, this film is a eulogy. If you can treat it as its own thing, you might enjoy the ride.

Parental Guidance

Predator: Badlands carries a PG-13 rating, making it the first standalone Predator film appropriate for younger teens. Violence includes significant sci-fi action throughout with alien creatures stabbed, slashed, shot, and dismembered. A character is executed on screen. However, no human characters are killed, and the violence is presented without the gore of previous R-rated franchise entries. No sexual content. Minimal language with most dialogue in the constructed Yautja language. Some intense creature sequences may frighten younger children. Suitable for viewers 10 and up who enjoy sci-fi action. Parents of children under 13 should be aware of the feminist messaging and found-family-over-blood-family theme which directly contradicts traditional family values. Consider watching together to discuss the film's underlying messages.
